items.title: Google’s new Gemini 4 Argon equals GPT-6 Astra on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 60% ...
items.content:
Google’s new Gemini 4 Argon equals GPT-6 Astra on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 60% of the Cost per Task with discounted prices. Google is now back to being one of the top three labs in intelligence achieved

Gemini 4 Argon is @GoogleDeepMind’s first proprietary model above the Flash class in over 7 months. With high reasoning (the highest available), it scores 53 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, matching GPT-6 Astra (max, 53) and 1 point ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 52), with gains driven by lower hallucinations and stronger agentic capabilities.

At its current 50% pricing discount and with cache discounts increased to 95%, Gemini 4 Argon costs $1.99 per Intelligence Index task, 60% of GPT-6 Astra (max), but 2.7x GPT-6.1 Sol (max). After the discount ends, this will rise to $3.98 (~1.2x GPT-6 Astra (max)).

Gemini 4 Argon is currently being rolled out to selected users and is not publicly available. The 50% discount is an initial promotion. Google has not yet confirmed the promotion end date

Key benchmarking results for Gemini 4 Argon with high reasoning:

➤ Google returns as one of the top three labs on intelligence: Gemini 4 Argon (high) scores 53 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, matching GPT-6 Astra (max, 53) and 1 point ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 52). This is 23 points above Google’s previous non-Flash model, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (30) and 12 points ahead of Gemini 3.8 Flash (high)

➤ Launch discounts of 50% make Gemini 4 Argon competitive on Cost per Task: At current discounted pricing, Gemini 4 Argon (high) costs $1.99 per Intelligence Index task, 60% of GPT-6 Astra (max, $3.26) for a comparable level of intelligence. This cost efficiency is driven by lower token prices, rather than reduced token use, with Gemini 4 Argon averaging 62k output tokens per task, compared with 27k for GPT-6 Astra (max). Google has not yet confirmed the promotion end date, but on standard pricing, Cost per Task will increase to $3.98

➤ Stronger agentic performance: Historically a weaker area for Gemini models, Gemini 4 Argon shows improvements across agentic evaluations. It ranks #1 on AutomationBench-AA at 77.5%, 6 points ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max, 71.3%). On Terminal Bench 4, Gemini 4 Argon achieves 57%, a +53 point improvement from Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, only behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max, 64%), Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 60%) and GPT-6 Astra (59%). On AA-Briefcase, it reaches 1494 Elo. This is driven by a 65% rubric pass rate, the highest we have recorded, but lower Analytical Quality (1576 Elo) and Presentation Quality (1308 Elo)

➤ Lowest hallucination rate among leading models: On AA-Omniscience, Gemini 4 Argon has a 15% hallucination rate, the lowest of any model scoring 45+ on the Intelligence Index, compared with 51% for GPT-6 Astra (max) and 54% for GPT-6.1 Sol (max). This means Argon is much more likely to acknowledge when it does not know an answer rather than guess incorrectly. On accuracy, Gemini 4 Argon scores 50%, a 5 point decrease from Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, and 13 points below GPT-6 Astra (max, 63%). With this slightly lower accuracy, its overall AA-Omniscience score of 42 remains in line with GPT-6 Astra (43) and GPT-6.1 Sol (42)

Key model details:

➤ Context Window: 1M tokens

➤ Multimodality: Text, image, video, and speech input, with text output

➤ Pricing: $4/$20 per 1M input/output tokens at standard pricing, currently discounted 50% to $2/$10. Cached input tokens receive a 95% discount ($0.10 per 1M at discounted pricing), up from 90% on Gemini 3.8 Flash

➤ Long Decode Continuation: We tested Gemini 4 Argon with Long Decode Continuation, a new Gemini API feature that pauses long responses and resumes them across follow-up calls. This lets reasoning run up to 1M output tokens without request timeouts

SITUATION EXPLAINED: The frontier labs just agreed to outside auditors, and Jensen signed too.

• Th...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: The frontier labs just agreed to outside auditors, and Jensen signed too.

• The Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibility, signed by Trump, Sundar Pichai, Dario, Zuckerberg, Greg Brockman, Elon, and Jensen
• Every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely, which is Sacks's position, no new top-down regime
• Layer one: internal controls monitoring capability and alignment during training and deployment, covering cyber, bio, and chemical threats, and ensuring models do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways
• Layer two: an internal team verifying those controls are operating as intended
• Layer three: an independent external auditor running the same assessment, which means METR, Redwood, Palisade, or Faculty
• Layer four: an independent board committee receiving reports from both
• Trump signed an executive order the same day making superintelligence, SI, the official term across the executive branch. He called the accord morally binding

@theojaffee: "A lot of what the safety people wanted in terms of policy, they're getting now. And this was supported by many of the usual people who oppose these safety measures. I think they see the way the winds are blowing."

items.summary_html: Following yesterday's News coverage of the White House AI pact, An explainer on the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibility signed by Trump, Pichai, Dario Amodei, Zuckerberg, Brockman, Musk, and Jensen Huang: a layered framework of internal safety controls, internal verification, independent external audits (METR, Redwood, Palisade, Faculty), and board oversight — plus an executive order adopting 'superintelligence' as official terminology.
items.content_html:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: The frontier labs just agreed to outside auditors, and Jensen signed too.

• The Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibility, signed by Trump, Sundar Pichai, Dario, Zuckerberg, Greg Brockman, Elon, and Jensen

• Every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely, which is Sacks's position, no new top-down regime

• Layer one: internal controls monitoring capability and alignment during training and deployment, covering cyber, bio, and chemical threats, and ensuring models do not hack or access technical systems in unintended ways

• Layer two: an internal team verifying those controls are operating as intended

• Layer three: an independent external auditor running the same assessment, which means METR, Redwood, Palisade, or Faculty

• Layer four: an independent board committee receiving reports from both

• Trump signed an executive order the same day making superintelligence, SI, the official term across the executive branch. He called the accord morally binding

@theojaffee: "A lot of what the safety people wanted in terms of policy, they're getting now. And this was supported by many of the usual people who oppose these safety measures. I think they see the way the winds are blowing."

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: The FTC is investigating OpenAI, Anthropic, and METR, the group they hired to i...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: The FTC is investigating OpenAI, Anthropic, and METR, the group they hired to investigate themselves.

• It's a consumer protection probe, not antitrust, focused on unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act
• Chairman Andrew Ferguson started it weeks ago, before the Hugging Face incident. He was at the White House signing ceremony on Tuesday
• The agency is drafting civil investigative demands, effectively subpoenas, to compel executive testimony
• METR is a target too, which is strange given it's the organization both labs hired to investigate their own incidents
• Ferguson: "I think it's very important that we not allow these two firms to come to Washington, whip everyone into a panic, and then say, we need a whole bunch of regulations that we can comply with"
• He's also said companies can't shift legal blame to rogue AI systems when their automated decisions cause harm

@theojaffee: "METR is also expected to be a target of the probe. Really? What do they want from METR? That's interesting, actually."

items.title: Introducing Praxis-1, an open-weight World Action Model that turns our video pre-training expertise ...
items.content:
Introducing Praxis-1, an open-weight World Action Model that turns our video pre-training expertise into real world control for robots.

Robot demonstration data is limited. But video data is infinite. Praxis-1 extends our bet that the best policy models will learn from video, and use that scale to bring embodied intelligence to every industry.

Praxis-1 is built on our large-scale video pre-training and real-time infrastructure, and acts as a policy model for robotics developers and researchers that works across any embodiment or environment, no matter how complex.

We are actively testing with early partners including Noble Machines, Standard Bots and Ultra, and will be releasing the weights publicly in the coming months.

Learn more and request early access at https://t.co/DzCMQpYNXQ

items.title:
The model behind these characters is A1,

It's a real-time model that creates full-body AI character...
items.content:
The model behind these characters is A1,

It's a real-time model that creates full-body AI characters that keep listening while they talk and move. You can interrupt one of these characters mid-sentence and change the topic, and they will follow you.

I read their technical report, and the secret behind how A1 works is that it generates audio and video in small, continuous segments. They keep neighboring segments consistent and, that way, reduce the drift in the character and scene over time.

Utopai X (based on MiniMax H3) debuts at #2 on the Artificial Analysis Text to Video Leaderboard, behind only Wan 3.0

Utopai X is the new video model from Utopai Studios, post-trained on MiniMax H3 and launching today inside PAI, Utopai’s cinematic storytelling web platform. Utopai Studios is an AI-native film and TV studio, with three wide theatrical release films and two series scheduled for release in 2027.

In AA-Video-T2V v2.0, our refreshed Text to Video with Audio leaderboard, Utopai X ranks #2, behind Wan 3.0 and ahead of Dreamina Seedance 2.5. As of today, it is the highest ranked of the three models on the leaderboard built on MiniMax H3, ahead of MiniMax H3 itself and fal's MiniMax H3 Max.

Utopai X is available in PAI at 93 PAI credits per second of video, with no public API. PAI plans start at $15 per month (billed monthly) for 1,000 credits.

Congratulations to @UtopaiStudios on the release!

See below for our analysis and example outputs of Utopai X in the Artificial Analysis Video Arena 🧵

items.title: We are launching AA-Video-T2V v2.0, our new benchmark for evaluating text to video models, alongside...
items.content:
We are launching AA-Video-T2V v2.0, our new benchmark for evaluating text to video models, alongside AA-Video-T2V-Silent v2.0 for video generation without audio. Built on a new methodology, it judges every model at 1080p on a regularly refreshed prompt set, and ranks them across 10 use cases, 10 capabilities and a wide range of styles.

Video models are being adopted across more industries and workflows, from film studios to advertising agencies. Our new benchmark not only ranks models overall, but also shows which model is best for specific use case and video generation capability. Use cases are grounded in how consumers and enterprises use video generation. Capabilities draw on lab and academic research, and on how creators and businesses push video models today. We tag every prompt by use case (such as Live-Action Film and Marketing & Advertising) and by the capability it tests (such as Text Rendering and Audio Synchronization), and the overall benchmark samples evenly across both. Because of this, the overall ranking reflects a model's versatility across use cases and well-roundedness across capabilities. We also tag each prompt by visual style, such as photorealistic, 3D render, cartoon and anime, and hand-drawn illustration.

AI video is also moving onto bigger screens and into production, from microdramas to movie theaters, while low barrier to generate is resulting in a proliferation of low quality AI video content. The quality bar keeps rising, so we now judge every clip at 1080p and high bitrate.

We are launching AA-Video-T2V v2.0 with more than 68,000 high quality human preference votes from private evaluators based in US/UK over 1,000 prompts, and AA-Video-T2V-Silent v2.0 with more than 47,000 votes over 500 prompts.

Initial insights from an in-depth analysis of the 10 highest ranking models on the Artificial Analysis AA-Video-T2V v2.0 Leaderboard:

➤ Wan 3.0 ranks #1 overall and leads 10 of the 20 category boards, including Cartoon and Anime style and Animation & Gaming use case, at $12 per minute of video.

➤ Dreamina Seedance 2.5 ranks #2 and is the human performance specialist, #1 on both Human Anatomy and Dialogue & Lip Sync. At $34.12/min it is the most expensive model in the top 10.

➤ MiniMax H3 (768p) ranks #3, statistically tied with Seedance 2.5 at $4.80/min, about 1/7 of the price. It is also #1 on Text Rendering.

➤ FLUX 3 ranks #4, with its strongest results on Text Rendering (#3) and Dialogue & Lip Sync (#2).

➤ Gemini Omni Flash 1.1 ranks #5 and is the graphic 2D and audio specialist, #1 on UI/UX & Motion Design use case, Flat Design style and Audio Synchronization capability.

See below for the use case, capability and style breakdowns 🧵

We tag every prompt by use case (such as Live-Action Film and Marketing & Advertising) and by the capability it tests (such as Text Rendering and Audio Synchronization), and the overall benchmark samples evenly across both. Because of this, the overall ranking reflects a model's versatility across use cases and well-roundedness across capabilities. We also tag each prompt by visual style, such as photorealistic, 3D render, cartoon and anime, and hand-drawn illustration.

AI video is also moving onto bigger screens and into production, from microdramas to movie theaters, while low barrier to generate is resulting in a proliferation of low quality AI video content. The quality bar keeps rising, so we now judge every clip at 1080p and high bitrate.

We are launching AA-Video-T2V v2.0 with more than 68,000 high quality human preference votes from private evaluators based in US/UK over 1,000 prompts, and AA-Video-T2V-Silent v2.0 with more than 47,000 votes over 500 prompts.

Initial insights from an in-depth analysis of the 10 highest ranking models on the Artificial Analysis AA-Video-T2V v2.0 Leaderboard:

➤ Wan 3.0 ranks #1 overall and leads 10 of the 20 category boards, including Cartoon and Anime style and Animation & Gaming use case, at $12 per minute of video.

➤ Dreamina Seedance 2.5 ranks #2 and is the human performance specialist, #1 on both Human Anatomy and Dialogue & Lip Sync. At $34.12/min it is the most expensive model in the top 10.

➤ MiniMax H3 (768p) ranks #3, statistically tied with Seedance 2.5 at $4.80/min, about 1/7 of the price. It is also #1 on Text Rendering.

➤ FLUX 3 ranks #4, with its strongest results on Text Rendering (#3) and Dialogue & Lip Sync (#2).

➤ Gemini Omni Flash 1.1 ranks #5 and is the graphic 2D and audio specialist, #1 on UI/UX & Motion Design use case, Flat Design style and Audio Synchronization capability.

See below for the use case, capability and style breakdowns 🧵

items.content:
To integrate an agent with any app:

Use the AG-UI protocol. AG-UI stands for "Agent-User Interaction Protocol".

Every big-name company is already using AG-UI: Anthropic, Google, AWS, Microsoft, LangChain, Mastra, Pydantic, etc.

This is the open, community-driven standard for how agents and frontends communicate.

Their new v1.0 is out. Here is what you get:

• It works with any frontend: web, mobile, terminal, etc.
• It works with any chat app: Slack, Teams, etc.
• It supports all types of generative UI: A2UI, MCP apps, etc.
• It supports subagents, shared state, interrupts
• End-to-end interaction data you can learn from

Their specification now supports a JSON schema to define events and how they behave: their order, run lifecycle, and errors. It's precise enough for anyone to implement.

If you have a custom agent or harness, you can write one adapter that outputs AG-UI events, and plug it into everything built on top. If you want to take your agent to production, @CopilotKit provides the full UI layer, plus threads, agent analytics, automatic learning, and more.

Full developer guide for AG-UI: https://t.co/eTs6HjfDZi

Thanks to the team for partnering with me on this post.

items.title: Oxide CTO @bcantrill says the people promising to "automate the economy" should spend a day in a fac...
items.content:
Oxide CTO @bcantrill says the people promising to "automate the economy" should spend a day in a factory, because much of the physical world isn’t even in the software loop:

"People would benefit from going, working in a factory, going to a mine. Go into the actual industrial economy that people are talking about. It doesn't work the way you think it does."

"It reminds me very much of the hysteria before Y2K. Ed Yourdon was saying that in New York City, you will not have water on January 1st, 2000, because there are microcontrollers that control the water system."

"They interviewed the person that runs the municipal water authority. He's like, 'Do you understand how water works in New York? Do I need to send you a memo on gravity? The water is in the Adirondacks. It flows down to New York City.'"

"People need to spend more time reading Richard Scarry. Learn how the world works, and then you can learn what the actual perils of automation might be and might not be."
@oxidecomputer

items.title: Recent advances in training LLMs with reinforcement learning rely on verifiable rewards, checking on...
items.content:
Recent advances in training LLMs with reinforcement learning rely on verifiable rewards, checking only whether the final answer is correct rather than evaluating intermediate steps. While this reduces reward hacking and human annotation costs, it introduces a major reliability problem: models often produce fragile, idiosyncratic reasoning paths that arrive at the correct answer by chance. Consequently, as systems generate multiple candidate reasoning paths to find consensus, standard methods frequently experience degraded performance and reduced consistency across samples.

This article from @MSFTResearch introduces and evaluates Reinforcement Learning with Transferable Reward, a new framework designed to ensure that intermediate reasoning steps are robust and reusable. 

The primary objective is to demonstrate that rewarding a model when its partial reasoning can be successfully continued and solved by a separate receiver model leads to higher overall accuracy, greater multi-sample consistency, and improved training efficiency without requiring manual step-level supervision.

Read with an AI tutor: https://t.co/RF86ePrDxO

Oxide CTO @bcantrill says AI extinction talk "escaped containment" from Silicon Valley, only to run into a basic question from family members:

how exactly does this lead to extinction?

"In the larger world, the commonsensical world, these arguments don't carry the weight that they do here in Silicon Valley. People have the natural question of, 'I'm a gym teacher in Little Rock, Arkansas, and I'm trying to understand how that would lead to my extinction.'"

"Nope, it does not lead to your extinction, and sorry, on behalf of everyone in Silicon Valley, sorry that we've let this escape containment into mainstream discourse, implying that you should be afraid for your life and the life of your kids."

"It's convenient to talk about x-risk and divorce it from the underlying humanity, but you're talking about my kids and my sibling, my mom."
@oxidecomputer

Gemini 4 Argon is here, taking first place on 13 of the 19 benchmarks Google ...
items.content:
A big day for Google!

Gemini 4 Argon is here, taking first place on 13 of the 19 benchmarks Google published against GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5.

A few standout numbers:

- DeepSWE (long real-world coding tasks) – 77.9%, vs. 74.2% for Opus 5.5 and 74.1% for Astra
- Vals Index (real work in finance, law, tax, coding) – 68.9%, vs. 67.0% for Opus 5.5 and 63.1% for Astra
- Output limit is 1M tokens, up from 64K

Argon also leads on tests for vibe coding, long context, and reading charts and long videos.

The release is limited to trusted cyber defenders in Google's Fairwind Program to start.

items.title: Oxide CTO @bcantrill predicted the iPhone almost perfectly in 2003, then thought it would flop, and ...
items.content:
Oxide CTO @bcantrill predicted the iPhone almost perfectly in 2003, then thought it would flop, and says AI doomers should audit their failed predictions before making bigger ones:

"Do predictions and write them down. Predictions tell you more about the present than the future."

"I made a three-year prediction in 2003 that Apple would introduce a new must-have gadget called the iPhone that would be a combination cellphone, MP3 player, and digital camera, which is exactly what they did. I also thought it was gonna be a flop."

"I had a bunch of operating system kernel people together every year to make predictions. Not one of us predicted cloud computing."

"What is frustrating to me about some of these doomsayers is, can you go back to some of your past predictions which have been wrong at this point? Kudos to Hinton for coming back and saying, 'I was wrong.' We need a lot more of that."
@oxidecomputer

items.content:
The Economist editor @ArchieHall says Britain may have built itself into one of AI’s easiest economic targets by relying on service exports while lagging at adopting technology:

"I'm pretty concerned about where Britain could end up, and I think that's evocative of where a lot of non-US rich world economies could end up in a world where AI is more economically disruptive."

"You have an economy that's very, very services exports dependent. Law, finance, insurance. And it's not a vastly dynamic economy. It's not been incredibly successful adopting technology over the past couple decades."

"More nimble AI-enabled competitors could very, very easily eat away at the export base of a lot of those services companies that really power the British economy."

"Britain does have a pretty strong AI sector, but it's not huge, and most of the British economy is things that are not AI and things that are pretty bad at adopting tech."
@TheEconomist

items.content:
Oxide CTO @bcantrill argues Geoff Hinton’s 2016 call to stop training radiologists shows why AI expertise doesn’t make you an expert in every field AI touches:

"I thought Jensen did admirably, but I thought the questions from Klein were honestly terrible. He was admonishing Jensen for not deferring to the expertise of AI experts, like pioneers like Geoff Hinton."

"Nothing against Geoff Hinton, but Geoff Hinton is not an expert in radiology. If you wanna weigh in on radiology, go spend some time with radiologists. Work a shift with radiologists."

"In 2016, Hinton says, 'We should not be training radiologists.' You can easily imagine an aspiring physician in 2016 who comes across this article from a putative expert and thinks, 'I'm not gonna do that.' Meanwhile, we need radiologists."

"This is true across so many of these domains where these guys weigh in on things that are not their domain of expertise."
@oxidecomputer

items.title: AI agents rely heavily on their harnesses—the surrounding prompts, control flows, tool interfaces, a...
items.content:
AI agents rely heavily on their harnesses—the surrounding prompts, control flows, tool interfaces, and memory management that wrap around a core language model. While modern research increasingly automates the refinement of these harnesses through recursive self-improvement, evolving an agent against a fixed set of training tasks frequently causes severe overfitting. Agents often memorize benchmark-specific details, chase evaluation noise, or accumulate bloated complexity, resulting in performance gains that collapse when the system is deployed on unseen, real-world tasks.

This article from @GoogleAI introduces and evaluates Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement (RRSI), a framework designed to enable automated harness self-improvement while ensuring that learned mechanisms generalize effectively to held-out environments. The primary objective is to demonstrate that applying statistical regularization principles to both candidate generation and candidate selection yields robust, reusable agent modifications without restricting what parts of the harness can be edited.

items.title: Functional gradient descent algorithms generally outperform neural nets, but are hard to accurately ...
items.content:
Functional gradient descent algorithms generally outperform neural nets, but are hard to accurately implement. This is because functional gradients are infinite-dimensional, and therefore must be approximated in practice; but if you approximate them naively, you converge to the wrong place.

To rectify this, the authors formalize a broad class of approximation schemes ("adaptive representations"), which provably ensure convergence to the global minimizer while being immediately implementable.

The resulting algorithms outperform corresponding neural nets often by an order of magnitude, across a number of settings.

items.title: Multi-turn AI agents powered by LLMs are essential for automating complex, multi-step tasks such as ...
items.content:
Multi-turn AI agents powered by LLMs are essential for automating complex, multi-step tasks such as software development, scientific research, and web navigation. Improving these agents requires reinforcement learning, which depends on generating thousands of interactive trial runs, known as rollouts, across external environments. However, existing training systems embed the execution and management of these rollouts directly inside the machine learning training loop. This tight coupling creates a severe operational bottleneck because input/output-heavy environment simulations interfere with compute-heavy model optimization, complicating migration across frameworks and slowing system scaling.

This article from @NVIDIAAI introduces and evaluates ProRL Agent, an open-source rollout infrastructure designed to resolve these bottlenecks through a "rollout-as-a-service" architecture. ProRL Agent fully decouples trajectory generation, environment orchestration, and evaluation from policy optimization by exposing them as a standalone web service.

items.content:
Oxide CTO @bcantrill says the future is full of things we can build but still won’t, because economics kills more sci-fi dreams than technology does:

"What does powerful even mean? We've already accelerated ourselves into science fiction as far as I'm concerned. This is science fiction. Let's call it what it is."

"I'm a bullseye Gen X-er. I've got my space Lego set. We were gonna have moon colonization. We were gonna have flying cars. We were gonna have jet packs. We were gonna have supersonic travel everywhere. None of that has come to fruition."

"My grandfather flew in a Concorde exactly once. He said it was very uncomfortable. It solves one problem, but it creates a bunch of other problems that we as a society are not that interested in. We don't want sonic booms all the time."

"Efficiency matters. The cost matters. The economics matter. People get divorced from the actual economics of these things, and economics is the driver of everything. Sometimes people chalk up to politics what is actually economics."
@oxidecomputer

items.title: Video diffusion models have become the standard foundation for high-fidelity video synthesis, but ge...
items.content:
Video diffusion models have become the standard foundation for high-fidelity video synthesis, but generating videos with them requires substantial computational power.

To reduce latency and inference costs, practitioners routinely create efficient variants through distillation, which relies on full fine-tuning of the base architecture. 

Meanwhile, low-rank adaptation—commonly known as LoRA—is the primary tool used to customize model styles and behaviors without retraining the entire system. However, when customization modules trained on a base model are directly applied to its distilled variants, they frequently suffer from severe visual artifacts, character duplication, and style degradation. Retraining these modules for every newly distilled model requires access to private user data and substantial computing budgets, creating an operational bottleneck.

The article aims to explain the mathematical mechanisms causing this incompatibility and to develop a data-free method that enables seamless transfer of existing customization modules to distilled video models without additional training.

items.title: Scaling reinforcement learning to enhance the reasoning capabilities of LLMs is currently constraine...
items.content:
Scaling reinforcement learning to enhance the reasoning capabilities of LLMs is currently constrained by major hardware and algorithmic bottlenecks. During the generation phase, models produce long, multi-step reasoning responses that vary significantly in length. 

Because standard training updates require all generated responses in a batch to finish before updating model parameters, faster responses sit idle while waiting for the longest ones to finish. This creates severe hardware underutilization, leaving graphic processing units idle for up to 70% to 74% of generation cycles.

The article from @MSFTResearch introduces SortedRL, an online length-aware scheduling system designed to accelerate training and improve learning efficiency without destabilizing the reinforcement learning process.

Read the paper with an Ai tutor: https://t.co/TtLSpoVaoa

items.title: AI agents can perform complex coding tasks over extended periods, but sustaining genuine scientific ...
items.content:
AI agents can perform complex coding tasks over extended periods, but sustaining genuine scientific research across long horizons remains an open challenge.

Iterative scientific discovery requires exploring competing directions, learning from costly failures, and using accumulated insights to refine future attempts. Most existing agent systems treat experiments as isolated, sequential trials or rely heavily on human intervention, which causes them to lose structural continuity and overfit to development feedback.

This article introduces and evaluates Arbor, an open-source framework designed for autonomous research under a setting called Autonomous Optimization. In this setup, an AI agent takes an initial research artifact—such as code, models, or data pipelines—and iteratively improves it toward a defined objective without step-level human supervision.

Read the paper with an AI tutor: https://t.co/TU9JJHJJNO

The Economist editor @ArchieHall argues AI dramatically raises the value of economic dynamism, making it far more costly for countries to protect unproductive firms and rigid labor markets:

"I'll sound a little bit like a writer from The Economist right now and say that all the free market liberal reforms we've always championed are even more necessary in the new age of AI. The returns to dynamism have gone up."

"If we're gonna be in a situation where a hell of a lot of stuff is changing very quickly and where a lot of new firms are going to emerge, then you want to have an economy that can do that. The answer isn't the government sponsors FDEs to go into every company in some top-down manner."

"You wanna make sure it's easy for firms to hire workers, and part of that also means make it easy for firms to fire workers. Britain's better than Europe on this, but not where the US is."

"We have a very long tail of unproductive small enterprises in Britain that are implicitly subsidized by the tax system. That's gonna be a lot more damaging in a world of AI disruption where you do want that churn."
@TheEconomist

"If we're gonna be in a situation where a hell of a lot of stuff is changing very quickly and where a lot of new firms are going to emerge, then you want to have an economy that can do that. The answer isn't the government sponsors FDEs to go into every company in some top-down manner."

"You wanna make sure it's easy for firms to hire workers, and part of that also means make it easy for firms to fire workers. Britain's better than Europe on this, but not where the US is."

"We have a very long tail of unproductive small enterprises in Britain that are implicitly subsidized by the tax system. That's gonna be a lot more damaging in a world of AI disruption where you do want that churn."

@TheEconomist

items.content:
The Economist editor @ArchieHall predicts AI may get so good at writing that we stop wanting the writing and just ask for the idea underneath it:

"I'm not a Luddite about most AI things. But I think on writing we should be pretty cautious."

"A lot of the objections people have to AI writing are to the sloppy, 'It's not this, it's that,' and it seems totally plausible that that falls away. For emails and admin and customer service complaints, it's probably already there."

"Writing is quite relational. There's a sense that you're reading something knowing there was someone at the other side of it, and there's a quality guarantee that comes knowing someone actually took the time to write this rather than just dashed off a prompt to their personal agent."

"In a lot of places, we're really just gonna want the prompt. If the writing's pretty good, there's no need to read a three-page thing if the AI produced it."
@TheEconomist

items.title: I've been actively fighting almost guaranteed age-related loneliness for years, studies show after a...
items.content:
I've been actively fighting almost guaranteed age-related loneliness for years, studies show after age 30 you start seeing friends less and when you get older especially men don't have any social life left!

It's preventable, but it takes effort and initiative

We've now organized 70 weekly coworking days where we meet with friends and work together, do show and tell, and try help each other make things (also hardware stuff more recently)

We've also started organizing movie nights, art nights, barbecues, we watched the World Cup final on a projector screen in the garden with friends

We did a collage night the other day where we bought cheap gossip magazines, colored paper, and Pritt glue, and gave everyone scissors to make their own art, I think nobody spent time on their phone for at least 4 hours, making things puts you in a flow state and it's fun to do it in a group because you talk about different stuff while making things than you would for ex having a dinner

Movie nights are nice too but less popular I think cause everyone prefers to watch movies alone and also you can't really talk during a movie

Coworkings range from having sometimes 20 people to sometimes just 2 people, people have their own lives, but me and @rameerez still try to organize them weekly

One thing I realized is that we are usually the ones organizing stuff, but that's not a bad thing, there's even studies about this, there's usually a few people in a group who organize most of the events

If nobody in your group organizes stuff, it doesn't mean nobody wants to do stuff, but you have to take the initiative to bring people together which isn't easy in a time where phones and apps and the internet are simply easier and cheaper dopamine than driving to a friends house for a party

You can start with a coworking day, everyone brings their laptop, and you provide WiFi and coffee, then later you can try more types of events

Having an active social life is just as important or in some studies even more important for health than physical fitness

After a nice party I feel tired but satisfied, I had fun and didn't spend time on my phone or computer but instead talked and laughed with friends etc.

We don't drink alcohol with very few exceptions and nor do our friends, so it's mostly just having really nice food and sparkling water or kombucha etc, and we don't really need alcohol, after a few hours it gets fun enough anyway!

So I recommend everyone, take initiative, and organize something and get people together, it'll be fun! 😊

Our refreshed Text to Video taxonomy measures 10 capabilities and 10 use cases, each with its own leaderboard. Capabilities are the model skills a prompt is written to test. They draw on lab and academic research, and on how creators and businesses push video models today.

Utopai X ranks first in Audio Synchronization and Physics, narrowly ahead of Gemini Omni Flash 1.1 and Dreamina Seedance 2.5. It ranks second in Lighting & Materials and Camera Control, behind Wan 3.0. Against MiniMax H3, the model it is post-trained from, it is closer to the frontier on seven of the ten capabilities, with the largest gains in Audio Synchronization, Camera Control and Physics.

➤ Audio Synchronization covers diegetic sound effects, background music and score, and on- and off-screen sound.

➤ Physics covers mechanics, thermal effects, material interactions, fracture and deformation, optics, cause and effect, and counterfactual physics.

➤ Lighting & Materials covers lighting, exposure, shadows, color temperature, texture, cloth, and hair and fur.

"Being able to take the humans off of that process and get them in front of customers, giving demos, talking about the technology much deeper, is where we see the future of how internally companies can transform."

@ElevenLabs

items.title: Example Use Case: Live-Action Film covers cinematic scenes, performances, establishing shots and fil...
items.content:
Example Use Case: Live-Action Film covers cinematic scenes, performances, establishing shots and film-style lighting and camera work.

items.title: Example Capability: Audio Synchronization measures whether sound effects, music and ambience match w...
items.content:
Example Capability: Audio Synchronization measures whether sound effects, music and ambience match what happens on screen, in timing and in kind.

For text to video (with audio) models, native audio generation capability is a differentiator in ranking. Gemini Omni Flash 1.1 leads, followed by Dreamina Seedance 2.0 and FLUX 3. Wan 3.0 leads overall but ranks #4 here, its weakest capability relative to the field.

Models still struggle with specific audio directions, often missing a requested music style or the timing of a sound, while the leading models follow those directions and render audio that fits the scene.

We also judge the same clips without sound for AA-Video-T2V-Silent v2.0, and the comparison backs this up: among the top 10 on AA-Video-T2V v2.0, the models strongest on Audio Synchronization and Dialogue & Lip Sync gain the most when sound is added, compared to AA-Video-T2V-Silent v2.0. Gemini Omni Flash 1.1 gains 55 Elo, followed by Dreamina Seedance 2.5 (+44), Dreamina Seedance 2.0 (+40) and FLUX 3 (+38).

items.title: The Economist editor @ArchieHall calls the West’s inability to build a "pathology of affluence," whe...
items.content:
The Economist editor @ArchieHall calls the West’s inability to build a "pathology of affluence," where richer societies become less willing to tolerate the disruption that growth requires:

"I think you can start with this being a pathology of affluence. If you are wealthy enough, you start to care about things like having your neighborhood look and feel the same."

"For most of the 20th century, someone like France was actually pretty good at mega projects. Very good at building high-speed trains. In the '70s was very good at building cheap nuclear plants, and they're living off that inheritance."

"It's one of those layer cakes of accretions, where at any individual point adding an extra requirement to consult or an extra step is pretty well intentioned, doesn't seem super crazy, and then you get the outcomes."

"Add up good intentions, throw in the fact that this stuff's pretty popular, throw in a dysfunctional state that isn't very good at pruning this back, and you end up where we are now."
@TheEconomist

Retrieval systems often split long documents into chunks, but this strips away the surrounding context.

Contextual embedding models fix this by encoding the whole document once and pooling chunk vectors afterward.

They are usually trained on one gold chunk per query.

items.title: Example Capability: Text Rendering measures legible, correctly spelled on-screen text that stays sta...
items.content:
Example Capability: Text Rendering measures legible, correctly spelled on-screen text that stays stable as the camera and scene move.

Text Rendering is the biggest separator on the board, with the widest spread of any category. MiniMax H3 (768p) leads, followed by Wan 3.0, FLUX 3 and Gemini Omni Flash 1.1. In contrast, Kling 3.0 models rank #20 and #21 of 27, more than 100 Elo below the field.

The top-ranked models already render short and long text cleanly, but animated typography and keeping text intact on a surface that flips or spins upside down are still unsolved.

items.content:
Now @ChapterPal has a separate AI tutor that helps the learner with solving exercises without solving them for the learner.

This exercise-specific tutor doesn't provide a full solution. Instead, it asks the learner to try to solve the exercise themselves and then send their full or partial solution to the tutor for validation, correction, or hints.

It analyzes your solution (or the part of it you managed to write), tells you where you are wrong, and gives you hints so that you can keep trying to solve the problem yourself.

The first hint it gives is grounded in the text of the book that precedes the exercise by showing you a relevant piece of the book where you should look to get an idea yourself. If you are still blocked, the tutor gives you the immediate next step in your partial solution.

You can provide your solution to the tutor by typing it into the chat panel or by using pen and paper and then using the camera on your mobile device or laptop to let the tutor "see" where you currently are.

The first book that supports the exercise tutor is Active Calculus (2nd Edition) by Matthew Boelkins (2025), which contains plenty of exercises and do-it-yourself activities: https://t.co/CgICs5npAf.

I will add the exercise tutor to other books in the upcoming weeks.

The feature is not very mature, so please send me your feedback if you see any issues.

To access this new exercise tutor, look for the exercises that have a graduation cap icon in the heading. Click on the hat and try it.

items.title: ElevenLabs CRO @ashleyekramer reveals how Eleven v4 targets the 2 dead giveaways of AI voice: flat e...
items.content:
ElevenLabs CRO @ashleyekramer reveals how Eleven v4 targets the 2 dead giveaways of AI voice: flat emotion and the robotic pause before it answers.

Ever had a late payment blow up your year-end tax calculation?

A payment due Dec 30 arrived Jan 10.
Eleven  days. That's all it took to unravel our year-end numbers because the payment was already factored into our tax calculation.

By the time we caught it, we were redoing work that should have been done.

This happens to small business owners more than anyone admits.

It's not a payments problem. It's a systems problem.

With @airwallex Agentic Business Accounts, agents can match and reconcile incoming payments automatically as they land. If something doesn't match, an agent flags it for human review within the rules and approvals you set.

The agent catches the problem. You decide what to do about it.

Exactly what I wish we'd had in December.

items.summary_html: @svpino describes handling low-confidence results differently per workflow: some are reviewed, others ignored, illustrated by his solicitation-email screener where anything above 90% confidence is trashed and the rest stays in the inbox.
items.content_html:
@julesmalin For some of my workflows, I review low-confidence results. For other workflows, I just ignore them.

For example, I have a workflow to screen out any solicitation emails. They aren't spam, but I don't want to worry about them either.

I classify them, and anything above 90% goes to the trash. Anything lower than 90% stays in my inbox.
